intro: A quiet broken chord supplies material for both the opening and its later transformations. Follow the change from unison statement to accompanied return, then the extended coda that interrupts its own drive before accelerating.
question: How much can Beethoven change while keeping the opening material recognisable?

cues.title: A bare broken chord
cues.text: The hands begin in octaves, outlining F minor without a chordal accompaniment. Beethoven repeats the gesture a semitone higher before answering it with short repeated notes. The opening’s small stock of shapes will supply much of the movement.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 2, opening systems: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0 . The report places the sparse, quiet opening before the level rise around 0:35; it does not identify individual notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Softness interrupted
cues.text: In the opening group, sudden forceful chords interrupt the quiet unison writing. Listen for the difference between a short attack and the space left after it: the rests and withdrawals keep the forceful passages from becoming a continuous block.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 2–3, alternates quiet statements with forte/fortissimo writing. Relative level rises from −28.2 dB at 0:30 to −16.1 at 0:35, with further contrasts through 0:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A later nickname
cues.text: “Appassionata” was not Beethoven’s title. Beethoven-Haus traces it to a four-hand arrangement published by Cranz in Hamburg in 1838; the word “appassionato” does not occur among the original sonata’s expression marks.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus work catalogue, naming and reception history: https://www.beethoven.de/en/work/view/5292968940404736 .

cues.title: Major becomes minor
cues.text: The second group begins with a dolce melody in A♭ major, but its continuation turns to A♭ minor. Listen for the altered colour of a familiar shape rather than a completely new tune: the gentler manner does not guarantee a stable major-key ending.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 3–4, supplies the dolce theme and subsequent minor-mode continuation. The 1:20 and 1:34 novelty peaks bracket this change of manner; the darker passage continues through the measured rise around 1:50–2:05.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: No exposition repeat
cues.text: The exposition subsides instead of being repeated. Its A♭-minor close gives way to an E-major version of the opening gesture, beginning the development. A familiar outline now starts from an unexpected harmonic position.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 4–5, has no exposition repeat and moves from the A♭-minor close into the transposed opening. The report shows the withdrawal at 2:20–2:25 and a quiet restart around 2:30; 2:28 is an approximate formal boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A work taking shape
cues.text: The surviving sketches place most work on this sonata in 1805. Beethoven-Haus dates its composition from 1804 to the first half of 1806, rather than treating it as the product of a single occasion.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus work catalogue, composition history and sketch chronology: https://www.beethoven.de/en/work/view/5292968940404736 .

cues.title: Fragments rather than restatement
cues.text: Through the development, listen for portions of the second-theme melody rather than a complete repeat of its exposition. Beethoven transfers its material into new harmonic surroundings and joins it to more active accompanying figures.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 5–7, develops both thematic groups, including second-theme material in the D♭ region. The report’s strong changes at 2:56–3:08 are followed by a quieter stretch around 3:20–3:35 and a renewed rise; this cue concerns the surrounding development, not a timed chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dominant holds
cues.text: Near the development’s end, the bass settles on C, the dominant of F minor, while the upper writing keeps moving. Diminished harmony and repeated figures prolong the pressure: the return is prepared by holding a harmonic destination in view.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 7–8, supplies the dominant preparation and continuing figures. The 4:08 and 4:12 novelty peaks and high relative-level windows at 4:20–4:25 anchor the broad build before the 4:32 return estimate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return with a bass
cues.text: The opening contour returns, but no longer in the exposed texture heard at the start. An insistent C beneath it keeps the dominant present even as the familiar F-minor material comes back. Recognition and harmonic release are not the same event.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 8, restores the opening over repeated dominant notes. The 4:32 boundary follows the development’s crest; the report shows a sustained lower level and reduced detected onset density through 4:35–4:50. Timing is provisional, not bar-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recording amid exile
cues.text: Schnabel recorded this sonata in London on 11 April 1933. That year he left Germany after the Nazis came to power, moving first to Italy; his later move to the United States came in 1939.
cues.evidence: Bloesch, Artur Schnabel: A Discography, entry 49 and session list p. 89, documents the session: https://schnabelmusicfoundation.org/comceptr/uploads/Artur-Schnabel-A-Discography-by-David-Bloesch.pdf . The Foundation biography documents the separate emigration chronology: https://schnabelmusicfoundation.org/musicians/artur-schnabel/ . No causal connection between the session and emigration is asserted.

cues.title: The second theme at home
cues.text: The dolce theme returns in F major, the major form of the home key. Its shape recalls the exposition’s A♭-major melody, but the change of tonal centre makes it part of the recapitulation rather than another departure.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 9, places the returning second theme in F major. The report’s 5:56 novelty peak, low brightness around 5:55–6:00 and subsequent level rise support the approximate 5:56 boundary; machine key labels are not used to identify the harmony.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Minor reclaims the phrase
cues.text: In the second group’s later continuation, F minor replaces F major. The earlier major-to-minor change is repeated in the home key, followed by forceful closing figures. A recapitulation can restore the tonic without supplying a consoling major conclusion.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 9–10, supplies the F-major to F-minor change and closing passage. The report marks a change at 6:10, then a substantial rise around 6:30–6:40. The cue describes that extended continuation rather than its first altered note.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A coda still developing
cues.text: The coda does not merely repeat a closing cadence. Opening material and fragments of the second theme are worked over again, including a move towards D♭ major. Running accompaniment keeps the argument active after the recapitulation has ended.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 10–12, gives the extended coda and its D♭-major second-theme material. The report’s low level around 6:55–7:00 followed by renewed activity at 7:05–7:20 anchors the approximate 6:56 coda boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The drive breaks off
cues.text: Near the coda’s interruption, the running figures give way to a slowing, suspended passage. Beethoven writes ritardando and Adagio before a fermata. Listen through the loss of motion: the pause prepares a faster continuation rather than the final release.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 12, explicitly marks the slowing and fermata before Più allegro. The 7:46 novelty peak precedes a decline from −12.3 dB at 7:45 to −33.2 at 8:00 and sparse detected attacks.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Faster, still in minor
cues.text: After the interruption, Più allegro restores motion in F minor. Material associated with the second theme is compressed into the faster continuation; increasing activity does not mean a change to the major mode.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 12–13, supplies Più allegro and the F-minor thematic continuation. The report shows renewed level and onset activity from 8:10, increasing through 8:30–8:35; 8:06 is an approximate restart boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A quiet first ending
cues.text: The final drive loses weight and settles into a quiet F-minor close. Follow the decay after the last attacks. This movement ends by withdrawing; the sonata’s finale will make a different kind of ending.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 13, ends with diminishing dynamics and a sustained F-minor close. Relative level falls at 8:40–8:50 and reaches the noise floor around 8:55; the complete analysed file lasts 539.4 seconds.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A cadence opens space for dolce
transitions.how: The bridge’s fast figures diminish and settle on the dominant of A♭. Beethoven then changes the texture: a connected upper melody replaces the opening’s exposed octaves and explosive chords, with accompaniment underneath. A♭ major is the relative major of F minor, but the new melody still grows from a broken-chord outline. The change of key and manner is therefore linked to the opening, not an unrelated lyrical insertion.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 3: bridge and dolce entry. The report’s low level at 1:15, novelty peak at 1:20 and lower brightness at 1:20–1:25 support this approximate join. Score: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0 .

transitions.title: A quiet ending becomes another beginning
transitions.how: The second group closes in A♭ minor and subsides. Beethoven does not repeat the exposition: the opening broken-chord gesture reappears in E major, beginning a new tonal route. The change preserves the contour while removing its original F-minor position. Sparse texture and renewed quiet make the connection audible before the development expands the fragments into more forceful writing.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 4–5, gives the A♭-minor close and E-major restart without a repeat sign. The report falls to −37.2 dB around 2:25 and resumes quietly at 2:30–2:40. The join at 2:28 is estimated from that withdrawal and score order.

transitions.title: The bass continues under the return
transitions.how: A prolonged C dominant and diminished harmonies prepare F minor. When the opening phrase returns, Beethoven retains the repeated dominant bass rather than restoring the original bare octaves. The listener recognises the theme before the bass has surrendered its pressure. The return is consequently a continuation of the retransition as well as the beginning of the recapitulation.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 7–8, supplies the dominant preparation and altered returning texture. The 4:32 novelty peak follows the high-level 4:20–4:25 windows; the report then shows a quieter, more sustained stretch. This is a passage anchor, not a precise first-bar identification.

transitions.title: The bridge now prepares F major
transitions.how: The recapitulation’s expanded bridge redirects the harmonic preparation towards C, the dominant of F. As the running figures fall away, the dolce melody returns in F major rather than A♭ major. Beethoven preserves the contrast of melodic line and accompaniment while changing its tonal function: the second group now belongs to the home-key area. Its later turn to F minor repeats the exposition’s major-to-minor process.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 8–9, supplies the rewritten bridge and F-major dolce entry. The 5:56 novelty peak follows the quiet 5:45–5:50 span; brightness drops around 5:55 and relative level subsequently rises.

transitions.title: Closing figures reopen the material
transitions.how: The recapitulation’s closing figures subside in F minor, but the continuing semiquavers prevent the cadence from becoming a final stop. Opening material is recovered in a lower register and second-theme fragments move towards D♭ major. Beethoven uses the coda as another developing passage: accompaniment, register and harmonic direction change while recognisable fragments carry across the join.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 10–11, shows the closing passage and developing coda. The report’s withdrawal around 6:45–7:00 and renewed rise at 7:05–7:20 support the approximate 6:56 join; no isolated attack is claimed.

transitions.title: A fermata releases faster motion
transitions.how: The coda’s running figures are interrupted by ritardando, Adagio and a fermata over dominant preparation. Più allegro then launches a faster F-minor continuation, reworking the second-theme shape instead of introducing a new closing melody. The written change of tempo separates the two spans, while their thematic connection makes the restart part of the same coda.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 12, marks the slowing, fermata and Più allegro. The report has sparse activity and low level at 7:55–8:05, followed by a sustained rise from 8:10. The 8:06 boundary is provisional.

facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
